content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper claims to develop a framework to convert any regression/classification model into an uncertainty-based risk-aware model suitable for the task at hand.  The framework proposes wrappers to the models for each risk-based metric, and a composability operation to combine the metric into a single metric for the task at hand.  The paper provides some examples of applying the framework to extract epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty along with some potential applications to use the framework.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: The strength of the paper is the recognition that many different facets of uncertainty are need to represent decisional risk for a given application.  The main weakness of the paper is that it does not describe any detail about how the metrics are composed from the ensemble of uncertainty measures.  Furthermore, it is not clear what is new in the wrappers as all the uncertainty metrics used in the paper were proposed by others and fit into the framework.  As a result, it is really difficult to appreciate the novelty of the work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is easy to read.  While the paper does describe a contribution in terms of creating a framework for risk-aware classification/regression of machine learning models, the details about the wrappers and the composability of these wrappers are very vague.  This makes it difficult to appreciate the novelty of the work.  The wrappers seem to be simply the implementation of the various uncertainty-based methods that have already been proposed.  Perhaps there is novelty in the composition of the wrappers, but without the details, one can not determine if there is a generalizable composition scheme that can be followed for a variety of tasks or whether one has to think hard about how to train the composition for any given task.  For the most part, the experimental results section seems to demonstrate the value of different uncertainty measures developed by others.   Perhaps the ensemble methods in the regression experiments is an advance, but for the reasons mentioned earlier, it is difficult to gauge this. The application section does not provide any new insights for those familiar with these uncertainty measures. While it is nice Caspa will be open-sourced, the documentation of what Caspa actually does needs to be much more transparent for the work to be reproducible. 

f minor note, Algorithm 1 is not completely clear. In line 7, p_i appears out of nowhere.  Is \hat{y} in line 6 supposed to be p_i?  In line 5, is the N supposed to be a T in the averaging?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a framework to combine different facets of uncertainty in a risk-based measure for various tasks.  The papers lacks details about how the uncertainty measures are combined, and it is difficult to understand the novelty of using uncertainty-measures already proposed by others. The experiments did not seem to expose any new insights.

content.confidence: 2: You are willing to defend your assessment, but it is quite likely that you did not understand the central parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors focus on proposing a framework (capsa) for extending models with risk-awareness, the authors demonstrate the ability of capsa to easily compose aleatoric uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty, and bias estimation together in a single function set, and show how this integration provides a comprehensive awareness of NN risk. However, the novelty is limited, and the proposed method is too straightforward. To some extent, the proposed method is a combination of previous techniques.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

  1. The authors conduct a large empirical evaluation, including applications.
 
  2. Many additional illustrations are provided, which are useful for understanding.

Weaknesses:

  1. Limited novelty. Uncertainty estimation has attracted extensive attention in recent years, but what I can find in this paper is only the description that has been proposed and defined by previous papers[1][2]. I don't think it is necessary to take so much space to describe three categories of risk since it is just a repeated description of the cited papers. In other words, instead of the background, the paper needs more novel content proposed by the authors.

  2. Straightforward framework. The authors aim to propose a framework to extend models with risk-awareness. However, the framework is just a straightforward usage of the previous methods [1][3][4]. I have no idea what question has been solved in this paper, and the contribution may be the risk estimation of models. However, proving the previous methods are effective for estimating risk seems not challenging.

  3. Weak theoretical analysis. ``Lastly, the model is jointly optimized using all of the relevant loss functions by computing the gradient of each loss with regard to the shared backbone’s weights ...''. What is the mean of ``jointly'', there is no definition of the loss function or formal description, does the ``jointly'' mean adding all terms of loss as the total loss? If so, can authors show the relationship between different metrics?


Other concerns:
  1. Some results are empty in the tables, but they can be estimated through experiments.
  2. Writing issues.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing is good but the novelty is not enough.
content.summary_of_the_review: I read this paper repeatedly to avoid missing something, however, I still cannot find any novel contribution of this paper. Indeed, it helps me review many previous methods and it could be a good technology blog or a discussion in workshop, but it is not novel enough or theory-solid as a paper of the main conference.

display_title: Official Review of Paper3186 by Reviewer nYo4

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes Capsa as a framework for risk awareness in deep learning. Risk is defined through different sources of uncertainty (i.e. epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty) and representation bias. The paper proposes a wrapper which takes in a deterministic neural network and uses a feature extractor, which is either the penultimate layer or low-dimensional embeddings, with appropriate model transformations (e.g. adding dropout layers for epistemic uncertainty) to enable uncertainty quantification. The framework relies on density estimation on the extracted features for representation bias, mean and variance estimation for aleatoric uncertainty and Monte Carlo dropout, ensembling and variational auto-encoders for epistemic uncertainty. The framework supports combining epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty through a Monte Carlo approach. The framework is illustrated for various empirical settings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Uncertainty estimation for deep learning is crucial for deploying deep learning safety critical settings. Despite its importance, the field in general is lacking common benchmarks and evaluation methods. This paper makes an attempt to standardize this and enable applications for detecting noisy and adversarial examples and mitigate data representation issues.

Weaknesses:
- The paper offers limited advancements over the state of the art in uncertainty modeling. The main innovation is the introduction of wrappers to move towards a unified framework for uncertainty quantification. Even though I like this idea, I am afraid the paper falls short on some aspects of the methodology. Some of my concerns in this direction are:
  * Uncertainty quantification enables a probabilistic interpretation of the predicted quantities, which can capture both bias and variance. Therefore, at a high level aleatoric uncertainty estimation should capture representation bias. I am worried that the compositionality of these two could duplicate such effects.
  * I like the idea of wrapping a model to quantify the risk in predictions. However, the wrapper applies changes to the model and the loss function. Given that, one might argue that the uncertainty obtained might represent this new model’s predictive uncertainty. I think the paper needs to establish that the final probability distributions are indeed representing the uncertainty in the original predictions.
- Experimental results section serve as an illustration of capsa and I think it is lacking a quantitative comparison of how the capsa results compare to other frameworks like https://github.com/google-research/robustness_metrics and https://github.com/google/uncertainty-baselines. Furthermore, some empirical experiment results lead to further questions and need more discussion to establish rigor in the experiments:
  * The calibration plots in Figure 6 (especially Figure 6C) and Figure 9 suggest poor calibration from the uncertainty methods. However, other studies have shown that calibration improves with probabilistic approaches.
  * In Figure 5, the uncertainty in OOD data is lower for Ensemble + Dropout compared to these two techniques applied individually. I am a bit puzzled by this result since I was expecting this to have the opposite effect.
  * Figure 9. As the adversarial perturbation increases, the OOD detection becomes better and when perturbation is 0, the OOD detection basically follows a random pattern, which is counterintuitive. Could the authors comment on this?
  * Experiments shown in Section 3.2 are qualitative and the results shown might raise questions on cherry picking. 
- There is room for improvement for reproducibility, clarity and organization of the paper. 
  * The term “metrics” is being used in what I believe to be methods. In some experiments, I was not sure which metric was being used. Examples include Figures 4 and  5 (i.e. what is the uncertainty metric, is it variance?)
  * Details regarding experiments are missing, which hurts the reproducibility and interpretability of the experiments. For instance, in Section 3.1, how are the densities computed? How is bias computed?
  * Figures lacking labels and references from the text.
    * Figure 6E. Indicate IID and OOD.
    * Figure 5. Add the y-label for bottom plots.
    * Figures 1, 2 and 4 are missing references from the text.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Overall, the paper is well written but as mentioned above, with minor additions to the manuscript the clarity and reproducibility of the paper can be improved. These details include explanations of the experiment settings, which can go to an appendix. The term “metric” is used interchangeably with “methods”. A clarification of this can help improve readability of the paper.

The paper offers limited advancements over the state of the art in uncertainty modeling. The main innovation is the introduction of wrappers to move towards a unified framework for uncertainty quantification.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper offers limited advancement over the state of the art in uncertainty modeling. It is fair to evaluate the paper as an open-source framework contribution but even from this perspective, I believe the paper is lacking evaluations with respect to other similar frameworks. Because of this, I recommend rejecting the paper at its current form.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a framework capsa that tries to unify aleatoric uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty, and bias estimation and then helps the model to achieve risk awareness. Capsa is also claimed that the uncertainty estimates can be used for the downstream tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The main strengths: 
1. The paper discusses Representation Bias, Aleatoric Uncertainty, and Epistemic Uncertainty, which is relatively comprehensive compared with related works. 
2. Some experiment results are interesting and adhere the intuition.

The main weaknesses: 
1. Some sentences are hard to follow, such as: capsa modifies the existing network according to metric-specific modification. There are several typos indicating the paper needs more proofreading.
2. The assumption used in the proposed algorithm should be verified at least by some empirical experiments.
3. Are there any references that also use MVE to estimate the aleatoric uncertainty?
4. The model uses a shared feature extractor to achieve unifying all kinds of uncertainty metrics. The idea is simple but the implementation is unclear. How to build the feature extractor? 
5. It is hard to say whether the same model structure is a proper choice for all kinds of features, and it is also hard to determine each loss's weights when optimizing all the relevant losses together.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper needs more proof-reading. The assumption used in the paper needs to be supported by experiments of references.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents a framework capsa that tries to unify aleatoric uncertainty, epistemic uncertainty, and bias estimation and then helps the model to achieve risk awareness. The design of the proposed method is not well-motivated. Some of the key component  such as feature extractor needs more description.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
